chunks: That which the Sheikh — may God support him — informed me of, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa and al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from a group who heard him say:
Verily, smiling during salat does not invalidate the salat, nor does it invalidate the wudu. What breaks [the salat] is only laughter that involves qahqaha (audible guffawing).

His statement 'what breaks is only laughter that involves qahqaha' refers to [breaking] the salat, not the wudu. Do you not see that he said 'what breaks is only laughter that involves qahqaha' — and the word 'break' (qat') is only ever used in reference to salat, because it is not customary to say 'my wudu was cut off'; one says rather 'my prayer was cut off.' This is further corroborated by [what follows].

key_terms.اَلتَّبَسُّمُ: smiling — a gentle, soundless smile; distinct from audible laughter
key_terms.اَلْقَهْقَهَةُ: qahqaha — loud, audible guffawing; the legally significant threshold of laughter
key_terms.يَقْطَعُ: cuts off, breaks — the technical term for interrupting salat
key_terms.يَنْقُضُ: nullifies, invalidates — the technical term for breaking wudu

ai.seo_question: Does smiling or laughing during salat break the prayer or invalidate wudu according to Shia hadith in Tahdhib al-Ahkam?
ai.summary: This hadith from Tahdhib al-Ahkam establishes that smiling during salat invalidates neither the prayer nor the wudu, while laughter involving qahqaha (audible guffawing) does break the salat. Sheikh al-Tusi appends a jurisprudential gloss arguing that the verb yaqta' (to cut/break) is linguistically bound to salat and not wudu, since convention dictates one says 'my prayer was cut off,' never 'my wudu was cut off.'
